catalog_quote: Final stress avoidance results in a stress lapse at the right edge of a word containing an odd number of syllables. Languages displaying this type of stress lapse at the right periphery include Pintupi (Hansen and Hansen 1969, 1978) ... stress on odd-numbered non-final syllables counting from the left (Hansen and Hansen 1969, 1978). Examples of stress in Pintupi appear in (24). a. tjútaja 'many' …
sweep_summary: Three title hits for Pintupi-Luritja. (1) Pensalfini 2000 (ALS99 proceedings) was recovered from the the Internet Archive, read in full, and states the Pintupi pattern explicitly: initial stress, every second syllable thereafter, never final, morpheme boundaries ignored, with footed examples -- this CONFIRMS the catalog's binary+lapse fixed-strict coding, but it is secondary (data via Kenstowicz 1994 from Hansen & Hansen 1969). (2) Hammond 1986 NLLT is paywalled (DOI 10.1007/BF00133844; no OA copy via OpenAlex/Unpaywall/Semantic Scholar/author pages); its open sibling 'Obligatory Branching Revisited' (scanned here) never mentions Pintupi, so the 1986 paper's Pintupi content is unverified and at most a theoretical reanalysis; low priority. (3) Sayers 1990 (Notes on Literacy 63:47-50, read via ERIC ED413792 on archive.org) is a literacy-teaching note about reading Pintupi long words in 2-3 syllable rhythmic groups and says nothing about where stress falls -- silent. No item contradicts or refines the catalog; the underlying primary source Hansen & Hansen 1969 (DOI 10.2307/3622818) remains unread (JSTOR paywall).org APIs by automated download.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement and type as the catalog record (fixed-strict stress placement coded per word length as 10 100 1010 10100 (1 = a stressed syllable): initial primary, alternating secondaries, final-stress avoidance) and as the Pensalfini 2000 statement held by the project; Hammond's data and generalization are explicitly taken from Hansen & Hansen 1969, so this is another secondary restatement of the same primary source, adding the metrical analysis (extrametrical final syllable, left-headed feet L->R, left-headed word tree, bounded quantity-insensitive feet). Only snippets were readable; no full open copy exists.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the first syllable; secondary stresses on every other syllable after it (3rd, 5th..), but the word-final syllable is never stressed. Hammond derives it with final-syllable extrametricality, left-headed (trochaic) binary feet built left to right, and a left-headed word tree; he classes Pintupi feet as bounded (maximally binary) and quantity-insensitive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: alternating secondary stresses on odd-numbered non-initial syllables counting from the left, none on the ultima (so odd-parity words end in a lapse): exactly the catalog's stress placement coded per word length as 10 100 1010 10100 101010 (1 = a stressed syllable) pattern
new_statements.exceptions: only 'the ultima is never stressed'; the fragment view does not show whether Hammond discusses any lexical or morphological exceptions (the sentence continues beyond the visible fragment)
new_statements.identity_note: Hammond treats 'Pintupi' as described by Hansen & Hansen (1969), i.e. the Pintupi(-Luritja) of Papunya, NT (data collected 1967-68); no separate Luritja variety is distinguished.

audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-strict, initial primary stress, secondary on odd non-final syllables) is the textbook Pintupi pattern and the deciding Gordon 2002:525 quotation is verbatim in the. Heinz 2023 (downloaded now) reproduces the Hansen & Hansen 1969 paradigm word by word and confirms both bullets. The weakness is that everything is second-hand from Hansen & Hansen 1969/1978, which we do not hold (JSTOR paywall / print only). The held Gray 2024 ANU thesis p.39, by a current Pintupi-Luritja specialist, independently confirms initial primary stress and the conventional secondary-stress description, so the primary-stress coding is safe; it adds a caution (Tabain et al. 2014 on Pitjantjatjara: no phonetic evidence for secondary stress) that could be recorded as a note on the secondary-stress string but does not change 'fixed initial'. sources.citation: Gray, James. 2024. Topics in Pintupi-Luritja syntax and semantics. PhD thesis, ANU (already held, re-read for this compilation)
sources.quote: "Primary lexical stress occurs on the first syllable. Usually, Western Desert languages are described as having secondary stress on odd numbered syllables following primary stress (with no stress on final syllables); however phonetic investigations into the closely-related Pitjantjatjara have concluded that there is no evidence for secondary stress, contra wide-spread claims to the contrary (Tabain et al., 2014)." fn.3: "As Wilmoth (2022) notes though, there are morphological complexities surrounding stress placement that were not taken into account by Tabain et al. (2014)."

The open sibling paper Hammond, 'Obligatory Branching Revisited' (NELS-type proceedings, ScholarWorks@UMass hdl 20.500.14394/36437, scanned here) discusses Eastern Cheremis, Komi, Khalkha, Aguacatec, Aklan, Lenakel and contains no mention of Pintupi or Hansen. At best the 1986 paper would re-analyse the Hansen & Hansen 1969 data, not add a first-hand statement.

sources.citation: Sayers, Barbara J. (1990). Reading with rhythm: a help in tackling long words. Notes on Literacy 63: 47-50 (SIL).
sources.quote: One of the assumptions I worked with from my Iwaidja experience (Sayers and Pym 1977) was that long words were made up of rhythmic segments of two or three syllables and, in Iwaidja at least, the boundaries were of more importance than the stress placement. From this experience [I tri]ed segmenting the Pintupi words into groups of two and three syllables. When I hit the right arrangement the word was instantly recognised. I would then make a mark at the boundary of the segments.
sources.note: A literacy-pedagogy note by a non-speaker of Pintupi about teaching adult readers to attack long Pintupi words by rhythmic groups of two or three syllables; it never states where Pintupi word stress falls and gives no Pintupi examples. The one stress remark (that some rhythmic groups may not begin on a stressed syllable) is attributed to Tiwi and Iwaidja, not Pintupi.
